meta.title: Who really said "A thorough knowledge of the Bible is worth more than a college education"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No Roosevelt source. The oldest credit to him is from 1941, and the newspaper record 1770–1963 has no instance of the sentence at all.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A thorough knowledge of the Bible is worth more than a college education'?
meta.ogDescription: Not documented as Roosevelt. The nearest older line on record is William Lyon Phelps’s — and it argues something different from what this sentence says.

answer.label: Not Theodore Roosevelt — no source in his works
answer.sourceLine: Nobody has produced a Roosevelt source. Wikiquote lists the sentence among his disputed quotations, giving as its earliest citation a 1941 book of Bible narratives — twenty-two years after Roosevelt died. It is absent from his works on Wikisource, and the Library of Congress newspaper archive covering 1770–1963 returns no instance of it. The closest older line we could actually read belongs to William Lyon Phelps of Yale, and it argues something rather different.

source.heading: What is actually documented

docMeta.dd: 1941 · Stepping Stones: The Complete Bible Narratives (per Wikiquote)
William Lyon Phelps of Yale, printed 1924
No instance found in two phrase searches

source.excerpt: A knowledge of the Bible without a college education is worth more than a college education without a knowledge of the Bible.
trail: Wikiquote keeps this out of Roosevelt’s sourced material. It is in the Disputed section, cited only as quoted in Stepping Stones: The Complete Bible Narratives (1941) Wikiquote — Roosevelt, disputed ↗.

Nothing resembling it is in his sourced material either. Wikiquote’s sourced sections carry exactly one scriptural reference from Roosevelt — he closes a passage on national character in “The Progressives, Past and Present” (1910) on the Proverbs line “Righteousness exalteth a nation” — and a full-text search of English Wikisource, whose author page for him lists more than 80 books, essays and addresses Wikisource — Theodore Roosevelt ↗, returns no instance of this sentence.

The newspaper record does not carry it either. Two phrase searches of the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America archive, which covers American papers from 1770 to 1963, each return zero hits: “knowledge of the Bible is worth more than a college education” and the shorter “Bible is worth more than a college education”. What the looser wording does return is advertising copy: a humour column in The Milwaukee Leader of 6 November 1928, page 6, mocking an advertisement that claimed a thorough knowledge of the set of books it was selling was worth more than a college education.

The nearest older line on the actual subject is not Roosevelt’s. A syndicated feature of Bible testimonials in The Keowee Courier (Pickens Court House, South Carolina) of 3 September 1924, page 7, credits William Lyon Phelps of Yale University with the sentence quoted above. Whether the Roosevelt version is a compression of it is our own reading and not something the record states — but it is the only documented antecedent we found. (We cite these two newspaper pages rather than linking them: the Library of Congress viewer refuses automated requests, so we could not confirm the links resolve for a reader.)
source.cutTag: William Lyon Phelps, printed 1924 — a different claim
source.excerptNote: This is not the sentence at the top of this page, and it does not say the same thing: Phelps weighs two combinations against each other, where the Roosevelt version simply ranks one thing above the other. It appears in a syndicated feature of testimonials about the Bible in The Keowee Courier (Pickens Court House, South Carolina), 3 September 1924, page 7.
source.rightsNote: No author has been established for this wording, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it. Roosevelt’s own published writings are public domain in the United States — but this sentence is not among them, so his death date settles nothing here. The 1924 and 1928 newspaper pages quoted above are public domain. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Theodore Roosevelt
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Roosevelt
author.bio: Theodore Roosevelt wrote more books than most professional authors and gave speeches almost continuously for thirty years, which leaves an enormous surface for invented quotations to attach to. He also spoke comfortably in moral and scriptural terms in public, so an improving line about the Bible sits on him without friction. Wikiquote’s page for him carries a long disputed section; this sentence is in it.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Roosevelt is a plausible host for this one and a poorly evidenced one. He quoted scripture from public platforms and wrote enormously, which makes the sentence hard to disprove by ear — and easy to check, once you look for the source.

items.why: Wikiquote files it as disputed, with a 1941 earliest citation Wikiquote ↗. A full-text search of English Wikisource, whose author page for him lists more than 80 books, essays and addresses Wikisource ↗, returns no instance — and neither do two phrase searches of the digitised American newspaper record up to 1963.

A syndicated feature of Bible testimonials in The Keowee Courier (Pickens Court House, South Carolina) of 3 September 1924, page 7, credits Phelps with “A knowledge of the Bible without a college education is worth more than a college education without a knowledge of the Bible” — an older line, on the same subject, making a more careful claim. Phelps was Yale’s Lampson Professor of English Literature and wrote a daily syndicated newspaper column, which is the kind of feature that credit appears in William Lyon Phelps — Wikipedia ↗. Whether the Roosevelt version was compressed out of his is our inference, not a documented link.

The frame — a thorough knowledge of X is worth more than a college education — was common enough by 1928 to be a joke: a Milwaukee newspaper column of that November ran it against a book-set advertisement. The construction was in the air, unattached to anyone.

misattribution.truthLine: Roosevelt may well have valued the Bible; that is not the question. The question is whether he wrote or said this sentence, and no source has ever been shown Wikiquote — Roosevelt, disputed ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to him
lead: Roosevelt is an unusually attractive host for a line like this. He published prolifically — Wikisource alone lists more than 80 of his books, essays and addresses — and he did reach for scripture in public: the 1910 address “The Progressives, Past and Present” ends a passage on private character on the Proverbs line “Righteousness exalteth a nation.”

So the sentence sounds like him, which is exactly what makes it hard to dislodge. It simply is not in anything he is documented to have written or said, and the oldest credit anyone has produced arrives twenty-two years after his death.
detailsBody: No Roosevelt source has ever been produced for this sentence.
Wikiquote’s earliest datable attribution is a 1941 book of Bible narratives — twenty-two years after he died in January 1919.
A full-text search of the whole of English Wikisource, whose author page for Roosevelt lists more than 80 of his works, returns no instance.
The Library of Congress’s Chronicling America archive (1770–1963) returns no hit for the sentence.
The nearest documented antecedent is a differently-argued line credited to William Lyon Phelps of Yale in a 1924 newspaper feature.
context.pull: It sounds like him. That is the whole mechanism.
